analysis.one_liner: Requires insurers to count drug-maker and charity copay assistance toward patients' deductibles and out-of-pocket limits.
analysis.headline: The bill sat in the Senate health committee for over a year; the committee held a hearing on it in March 2026 but has taken no vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Right now, if a charity or a drug company helps a patient pay a copay, many insurers don't count that help toward the patient's deductible or yearly out-of-pocket maximum — so the patient keeps paying out of pocket much longer. This bill would change federal rules so that all such assistance counts toward deductibles, copays, and out-of-pocket limits, especially for expensive specialty drugs. It was introduced by Senator Roger Marshall with a bipartisan group of cosponsors and referred to the Senate health committee, which held a hearing in March 2026 but has not voted on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients who need expensive prescription drugs — especially specialty drugs like cancer or rare-disease treatments — and who receive copay assistance from charities or drug manufacturers. Under current rules, that assistance often doesn't count toward their deductible or out-of-pocket maximum, so they can pay thousands more before insurance starts covering costs. This bill would make every dollar of that assistance count.

how_it_helps.text: Requires that amounts paid by or on behalf of a patient—including assistance from non-profits and drug manufacturers—count toward deductibles, coinsurance, copayments, and out-of-pocket limits.
The counting rule specifically covers specialty drugs and drugs subject to utilization management, the categories where copay assistance is most common and cost-sharing highest.
Creates a tax-code safe harbor so counting assistance toward the deductible does not disqualify a plan from being a high-deductible health plan usable with health savings accounts.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and, through premiums, all enrollees would absorb some of the cost of expensive drugs that copay cards currently stop at the deductible. Drug manufacturers would also face pressure, since counting their assistance toward cost-sharing reduces the discount insurers get from the current arrangement.

drawbacks.text: Because cost-sharing structures are largely actuarially neutral, letting manufacturer assistance count toward deductibles can shift drug costs from the sickest patients to all enrollees through higher premiums.
The bill explicitly leaves prior authorization and step therapy untouched, so patients can still face delays before getting specialty drugs regardless of how copay assistance is counted.
The protection applies only to people with insurance coverage; the uninsured get no help, since no plan cost-sharing exists for assistance to count against.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit—copay assistance actually counting toward deductibles—is real and targeted at the sickest insured patients, and it preserves insurers' utilization-management tools. The drawback is modest but real: most cost-sharing structures are actuarially neutral, so blocking copay cards from filling deductibles shifts some costs to premiums for everyone; the bill accepts that trade-off. The bigger limitation is scope: it does nothing for the uninsured or for people whose plans cover none of the drug.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in March 2025 and referred to the Senate health committee, which held a hearing in March 2026 but never voted, so it has not reached the full Senate.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on March 5, 2025 and referred the same day to the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
The committee held hearings on the bill on March 19, 2026, but no markup or vote has been reported.
It has 27 Senate cosponsors: 20 Democrats, 7 Republicans, and the Republican lead sponsor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Patients with high drug cost-sharing are still waiting; the delay leaves the current system in place, which suits health insurers and benefits manufacturers who rely on copay cards to keep list prices high.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insurers and drug makers, for now

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship is genuinely bipartisan: a Republican lead with 20 Democratic and 7 Republican cosponsors, and no visible opposition actor in the record.

industries.note: Insurers can no longer use copay-card money to fill up deductibles before coverage starts, which protects their sickest customers but prevents them from offsetting the cost of expensive drugs through enrollee cost-sharing. Insurers' premiums may rise for everyone as a result.

The bill treats manufacturer copay assistance like patient money that counts toward cost-sharing, which makes copay cards more useful to patients and lets manufacturers keep list prices high while subsidizing insured patients' out-of-pocket costs. Independent research generally argues this entrenches high list prices, but the entrenchment here is of insurer cost-sharing design as much as of manufacturers.
Employer plans must change how they count cost-sharing for plan years starting in 2026, an administrative and cost adjustment with no offsetting benefit to the plan sponsor.

analysis.trajectory: The committee has held a hearing, which is a step beyond most bills that die quietly in referral, but no markup or vote is scheduled. With bipartisan sponsorship it could in principle advance, but a single senator's hold or committee inaction could keep it off the floor for the rest of the Congress; most bills at this stage do not become law.
